# Y8960 BASIC Extension Reference

> This is an English translation of the [Japanese original](../basic-reference.md). Where the two differ, the Japanese version is authoritative.

The specification of the statements and MML that Y8960 BASIC Extension adds to MSX BASIC.

## Device numbers and channels

The device numbers and channel numbers that `MASSIGN` and `MPLAY` take.

| Number | Device | CH | Notes |
|--:|---|---|---|
| 0 | SSGS | 0-5 | |
| 1 | OPLLEX | 0-8, 10 | 0-8 FM / 10 rhythm. 6-8 and 10 cannot be used at the same time (below) |
| 2 | OPL2EX | 0-10 | 0-8 FM / 9 ADPCM / 10 rhythm. 6-8 and 10 cannot be used at the same time (below) |
| 3 | SCC | 0-4 | |
| 4 | OPM | 0-7 | |

5-7 are not used. Specifying one gives `Illegal function call`.

**It cannot be used together with an MSX-AUDIO cartridge.** The OPL2EX is played through the same ports as MSX-AUDIO, and it appears on those ports only when, at cartridge startup, no other sound chip responds there.

### Rhythm mode

Each block of the OPLLEX and the OPL2EX uses channels 6-8 for the rhythm sounds while it plays the rhythm sounds of channel 10 (rhythm mode). **In one block, channel 10 and channels 6-8 cannot be used at the same time.**

**Whichever is assigned first takes precedence.** If some track holds channel 10 of a block, a `MASSIGN` to 6-8 of the same block is an error.
The reverse is the same, and it is the same within a single sequence. `MLOAD` and `MPLAY` are errors under the same rule.

**The mode is decided when playback starts.** When `MSTART` starts playing a sequence from the beginning, a block that has a track on channel 10 enters rhythm mode, and a block that has a track on 6-8 leaves rhythm mode. A block with neither stays as it is. `MPLAY` does the same when it starts playing. Right after `MINIT`, no block is in rhythm mode.

When a block enters rhythm mode, the pitch of the rhythm sounds (the F-Number of channels 6-8) and the volume of the rhythm sounds (`V`, per-instrument volumes such as `@B`, and `@A`) are set to their defaults. Because the OPL2EX has no rhythm sounds in the chip, it also loads rhythm voices into channels 6-8.

**Resuming from a pause and returning to the beginning on a repeat do not set the mode again.**
If the `Y` command rewrites the rhythm mode bit or the F-Number of channels 6-8 during playback, that value carries over into the next pass.

## Switching page 1

The cartridge carries five BASIC extensions, and only one of them appears in page 1 at a time. At power-on and right after a reset, it is MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2.

| Statement | Destination |
|---|---|
| `CALL MINIT` | Y8960 BASIC Extension |
| `CALL MUSIC` | MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 |
| `CALL AUDIO` | MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite |
| `CALL OPM` | OPM BASIC Extension |
| `CALL MIDI` | MIDI Play BASIC Extension |

On a switch, the hooks and work area of the BASIC extension that was switched in until then are released automatically. If it was playing, playback stops.

**The extension switched to sets all six hardware mixer values to 128.** However, MIDI Play BASIC Extension does not play the cartridge's sound chips, so switching to it leaves the mixer as it is. [`CALL MIXER`](#call-mixermaster-ssgs-opllex-opl2ex-scc-opm) can be used with the same syntax whichever one other than MIDI Play BASIC Extension is switched in, and it can also be used before each one's initialization statement (`CALL MUSIC` and so on).

The five in the table are accepted whichever BASIC extension is switched in.

What OPM BASIC Extension plays is the Y8960's OPM. What MIDI Play BASIC Extension plays is a MIDI interface in another slot, not a Y8960 sound chip.

## Statements

### CALL MINIT[(*resolution*)]

Switches Y8960 BASIC Extension into page 1 and starts using it. The same holds when it is executed while another BASIC extension is switched in. When the argument is omitted, do not write the parentheses either (`CALL MINIT`).

| Argument | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Resolution | 0-2 | Period of the interrupt that advances playback. 0 is about 60Hz, 1 is about 100Hz, 2 is about 200Hz. 2 when omitted (below) |

Panning is set per channel with the MML `i`*n* ([Panning](#panning--in)).

Rhythm mode is not chosen by an argument. It is decided by the channels the sequence uses ([Rhythm mode](#rhythm-mode)).

**`MINIT` may be executed again when `MINIT` has already been done.** In that case it first does the same as `MEXIT`, then initializes again. Playback stops, and everything that `MINIT` returns to its initial state goes back to it: sequences, the voices and waveforms you made, voice file settings, and so on. The new argument takes effect as given. If the argument is out of range, nothing changes and the result is `Illegal function call`.

#### Resolution

**The speed of a song does not depend on the resolution.** `T` decides the tempo; the resolution decides "how often the playback engine is woken up." The same song plays for the same length at any resolution.

Two things change: **the load as seen from a BASIC program**, and **the fineness of time**.

| Resolution | Period | Interrupts | Time granularity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | about 60Hz | **No increase.** It piggybacks on the VDP interrupt that the MSX computer already generates | 1/60 second |
| 1 | about 100Hz | 100 more per second | 1/100 second |
| 2 | about 200Hz | 200 more per second | 1/200 second |

**`0` adds no interrupts.** When playing while a BASIC program runs, this is the lightest. In exchange, note starts fall on a 1/60-second grid, so fine notes at fast tempos waver.

**On PAL machines, `0` becomes 50Hz.** That is because the MSX computer's VDP interrupt is 50Hz.

**`2` is the finest and the heaviest.** It is the default when omitted — if the machine is only playing music, taking the fineness with this is the straightforward choice.

```basic
CALL MINIT              ' 200Hz
CALL MINIT(0)           ' piggybacks on the VDP interrupt; BASIC stays light
```

### CALL MEXIT

Finishes using the BASIC extension. No arguments. Releases the hooks and work area and returns to the state before `MINIT` was executed.

### CALL MASSIGN(*sequence*, *track*, *device*, *channel*)

Assigns a device channel to an MML track.

| Argument | Range |
|---|---|
| Sequence number | 0-3 |
| Track number | 0-15 |
| Device number | 0-4 |
| Channel number | Depends on the device (table above) |

**There is a limit to how much MML one track can hold.** When assigned, a track receives one 2KB buffer, and an `MTRK` that no longer fits there gives `Illegal function call`. One note is about 2 bytes of bytecode, so **the rule of thumb is about 870 notes per track**. Split a song that exceeds this into several tracks.

**A sequence that uses voices takes one more buffer.** For FM sound chip presets, SCC preset waveforms, and those made with `VOICE COPY` and `WAVE COPY`, `MTRK` keeps a copy inside the sequence — this buffer is the place for those copies: one per sequence, up to 32 voices. It is returned by `MFREE` and by `MCLEAR` with the track omitted.

**Copies of OPM voices are kept separately from this.** Up to 32 per sequence, not counted among the 32 for OPLLEX, OPL2EX and SCC. Their location is fixed, and they take no buffer.
**Writing notes on an FM sound chip or SCC track uses this even if you do not write `@`*n*** — notes play with `@0`, and `@0` also has a record to be copied.

Specifying a device channel that is already assigned is an error. Specifying a channel number the device does not have gives the same error. On the OPLLEX and OPL2EX, an assignment that would make channel 10 and channels 6-8 of the same block belong to different tracks is also an error ([Rhythm mode](#rhythm-mode)).

**Assigning initializes the track's playback data.** If you reassign after registering with `MTRK`, the registered playback data is lost. This is because the form of playback data differs by device family (FM sound chips / PSG sound chips), so it is not necessarily readable after the reassignment.

**Assigning stops playback of that sequence.** This is because the sequence being played would be reading playback data that is about to disappear.

**If you specify a device channel that `MPLAY` is using, the `MPLAY` playback stops and the assignment succeeds.** It is not an error. The same applies when you specify channels 6-8 of a block whose channel 10 `MPLAY` is playing (and the reverse).

A `MASSIGN` that ends in an error changes nothing. Playback continues, and the existing assignments and playback data remain as they were.

### CALL MFREE[(*sequence*[, *track*])]

Releases the channel assignment of an MML track and initializes the track buffer.
Sequence number 0-3, track number 0-15. When the track number is omitted, all tracks in the sequence are affected; when both are omitted, all tracks of all sequences are affected.
Specifying a sequence or track with no data is allowed.

**Releasing stops playback of the sequence that contains the affected track.** Even when only one track is specified, that whole sequence stops.

### CALL MTRK(*sequence*, *track*, *MML string*)

Registers playback data on an MML track. Sequence number 0-3, track number 0-15.

**Assign a device with `MASSIGN` first.** The form of playback data differs by device family (FM sound chips / PSG sound chips), so specifying a track with no assignment gives `Illegal function call`.

### CALL MSTART(*sequence*[, *repeat*])

Plays sequence data in the background. Specifying a sequence with no data is an error.

| Argument | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence | 1-15 | Bitmap (below) |
| Repeat count | 0-255 | 0 repeats forever. 1 when omitted |

#### Specifying sequences

**`MSTART` `MPAUSE` `MMUTE` `MSTOP` specify sequences as a bitmap.**
bit0 is sequence 0, bit3 is sequence 3. `&B0001` is sequence 0, `&B0101` is sequences 0 and 2. 0 and values of 16 or more give `Illegal function call`. Other statements (`MSTAT``VOLUME` and so on) specify a sequence by number (0-3).

**The specified sequences are operated on together.** The operation is applied to all of them before playback advances at all in between.

**If even one of the specified sequences meets an error condition, the result is an error and none of the sequences change.**

```basic
CALL MSTART(&B0011)     ' play sequences 0 and 1 together
CALL MSTOP(&B1111)      ' stop all four
```

Only the first time, the track buffers are packed to create sequence data before playback. A sequence paused with `MPAUSE` resumes from the point where it was paused.
The repeat count is counted when the end of the sequence is reached on all tracks, or when *(FINE)* or *(DC)* in the sequence is reached.
Therefore, if another track still has sequence data after *(DC)*, *(FINE)* is reached, that data is not played and the sequence repeats.

### CALL MPAUSE(*sequence*)

Pauses playback of sequence data. *sequence* is a bitmap ("Specifying sequences" under `MSTART`). `MSTART` resumes from the point where it was paused.
A sequence that is not playing, or a sequence with no data, is an error.

### CALL MMUTE(*sequence*[, *mute*])

Mutes the specified sequences. When muting starts, the volume values of the device channels in the sequence are overwritten with the minimum. The sequence keeps advancing while muted, but a muted sequence generates no note-on, and writes to the volume registers are overwritten with a value meaning silence. However, direct writes by the Y command pass through the mute.
A sequence that is not playing, or a sequence with no tracks at all, is an error.

| Argument | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence | 1-15 | Bitmap ("Specifying sequences" under `MSTART`) |
| Mute | 0-1 | 0 unmute / 1 mute. 1 when omitted |

The sequence keeps advancing while muted, so when unmuted, sound comes out from the playback position at that time.

### CALL MSTOP(*sequence*[, *fade-out seconds*])

Stops playback.

| Argument | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence | 1-15 | Bitmap ("Specifying sequences" under `MSTART`) |
| Fade-out seconds | 0-127 | 0 when omitted |

Stops the sequence while lowering its volume over the specified number of seconds, and ends playback when it reaches 0. What is lowered is the sequence volume, the same one as [`VOLUME`](#call-volumesequence-volume); the `MIXER` values (including the master) are not affected.

### CALL MSTAT([*sequence*, ]*variable name*)

Gets the current playback state. Stores 1 in *variable name* if the specified sequence is playing, otherwise 0. When the sequence number is omitted, all sequences are checked, and the result is 1 if any of them is playing.
Specifying a sequence with no tracks assigned is allowed.

### CALL MSAVE(*sequence*, *storage*, *parameter*)

Saves the current MML track data.

| Argument | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence number | 0-3 | |
| Storage | 0-2 | 0 array variable / 1 VRAM / 2 disk file |
| Parameter | | Array variable name, start address, or file name |

Write the array variable name without parentheses (`CALL MSAVE(0,0,A%)`). It must be a numeric array.
The VRAM address is `&H0`-`&HFFFF`. On MSX1, up to `&H3FFF`. Write addresses above 32767 with `&H` (in decimal they give `Overflow`).

**Storage 2 is a disk file** (`CALL MSAVE(0,2,"SONG.SEQ")`). The file name rules and errors are the same as `CALL EXPORT PCM` — a file with the same name is replaced, an invalid name gives `Bad file name`, insufficient free space gives `Disk full`, and a machine without a disk gives `Illegal function call`. If a disk error occurs in the middle of writing, the partly written file remains.

`MSIZE` tells the size that is written. **Specifying a size that the data does not fit in is an error, and in that case not a single byte is written.**

Specifying a sequence that has no track with a channel assigned is an error. When the storage is a file, no file is created.

**The voices, waveforms and software envelopes in use are written out with it.**
A sequence that is read back plays with the sound it had when saved, even if you remake them afterwards with `VOICE COPY`, `WAVE COPY` or `ENV COPY`.

For the procedure to save to a file, see "[Saving and loading data](#saving-and-loading-data)".

### CALL MLOAD(*sequence*, *storage*, *parameter*, *size*)

Loads sequence data. The arguments are the same as `MSAVE`, with the load size added at the end.

**With storage 2 (a disk file), *size* can be omitted.** When omitted, it reads up to the length of the file. When given, it reads up to the shorter of *size* and the file length.
If the file does not exist, `File not found`.

```basic
10 CALL MLOAD(0,2,"SONG.SEQ")
20 CALL MSTART(&B0001)
```

Specifying a sequence that already has MML tracks assigned is an error.
Also, trying to load a sequence that has a device channel overlapping a device channel assigned to an existing sequence is an error.
A sequence that would bring together channel 10 and channels 6-8 of the same block (whether between it and an existing sequence, or only within the sequence being loaded) is also an error
([Rhythm mode](#rhythm-mode)).
**In every case, that sequence is not touched.**

Specifying data that was not written by `MSAVE`, or data that claims to be larger than *size*, is an error.

**When loading from a file stops on a disk error, that sequence becomes empty.** No partly loaded track remains; it returns to the same state as after `CALL MFREE`.
The error is the one Disk BASIC raises.

### CALL MSIZE(*sequence*, *variable name*)

Stores in *variable name* the number of bytes that `MSAVE` writes out. Sequence number 0-3.
For a sequence that has no track with a channel assigned, it is 0.

```basic
10 CALL MSIZE(0,S)
20 DIM A%(S/2)
30 CALL MSAVE(0,0,A%)
```

### CALL MCLEAR[(*sequence*[, *track*])]

Initializes the playback data of MML tracks. Sequence number 0-3, track number 0-15. When the track number is omitted, all tracks in the sequence are affected. When both are omitted, all tracks of all sequences are affected. The assignments of the MML tracks are kept.

**The affected sequences stop.** This is because the data of tracks being played would be discarded.

### CALL MPLAY(*device*, *channel*, *MML*)

Plays MML immediately on the specified device/channel. Specifying a device channel already assigned with `MASSIGN` is an error. The other direction is not an error: a `MASSIGN` to a channel that `MPLAY` is using stops `MPLAY` and succeeds.

Specifying channels 6-8 of a block whose channel 10 is assigned with `MASSIGN` (and the reverse) is also an error ([Rhythm mode](#rhythm-mode)).

**It returns as soon as playing starts.** Playback proceeds in the background and stops when the MML has been played to the end. To stop it midway, use `MPSTOP`; to check whether it is playing, use `MPSTAT`.

**There is a limit to how much can be played at once.** The MML playback data plus the copies of the voices, waveforms and [software envelopes](#software-envelope--en) it uses must fit in 2KB. If they do not fit, `Illegal function call`. Voices and waveforms use 32 bytes each, and envelopes use 32 bytes per group of 8 numbers (0-7, 8-15, 16-23, 24-31). Copies of OPM voices are kept in a separate location, so they do not count toward this 2KB.

**Only one can play at a time.** A new `MPLAY` cuts off the playback of the previous `MPLAY`, even if the device or channel is different. `MEXIT` and switching page 1 also stop it.

**Loop commands cannot be used.** Writing `|:` `:|` `[`*n* `]` `(DC)` `(DS)` `(*)` `(TC)` `(CODA)` `(FINE)` gives `Illegal function call`. These are for sequences registered with `MTRK`; `MPLAY` ends playback at the end of the MML.

### CALL MPSTOP

Stops `MPLAY` playback. No arguments. Executing it when nothing is playing is not an error.
What `MSTOP` stops is sequences, which is separate from this.

### CALL MPSTAT(*variable name*)

Stores 1 in *variable name* if `MPLAY` is playing, otherwise 0. For the playback state of sequences, use `MSTAT`.

### CALL VOLUME(*sequence*, *volume*)

Sets the playback volume per sequence. Sequence number 0-3, volume 0-127.

**Every channel of that sequence goes down in volume by the same amount as the value is lowered from 127.** Each channel plays at its `@V` value minus (127 − volume), and anything below 0 becomes 0. One step of `V` corresponds to 4 of `@V`, so lowering `VOLUME` by 4 is the same as lowering `V` by one step (1 is 0.75 dB, one step is 3 dB). Every part goes down by the same number of steps, so the balance between parts does not change. The rhythm sounds' `V`, per-instrument volumes such as `@B`, and `@A` also go down by the same rule. On the SSGS, only the `V` steps go down; the channel volume set with `@V` (["`V` and `@V`"](#v-and-v)) stays as it is.

It is separate from the hardware mixer set with `MIXER` and does not affect the `MIXER` settings. This is what the `MSTOP` fade-out lowers.

It can also be set on a sequence that is not playing, and becomes the volume for the next `MSTART`.

### CALL MIXER(*master*, *SSGS*, *OPLLEX*, *OPL2EX*, *SCC*, *OPM*)

Sets the overall volume of the hardware mixer (master) and the output level of each block. Each volume is 0-128: 0 is silent and 128 is maximum (1-127 are proportional to amplitude). The values are written directly to the mixer registers and take effect immediately, even during playback. The OPL2EX value also applies to ADPCM. None of the six can be omitted. If even one is out of range, the result is `Illegal function call` and the mixer does not change.

**Switching to this BASIC extension from another BASIC extension sets all six to 128.** `MINIT` and `MEXIT` do not touch the mixer, so `MIXER` can be used after `MEXIT` and before `MINIT`, and the settings stay as they are.

For the per-sequence volume, use `VOLUME`.

It is separate from the SSGS channel volume (`@V`) and does not apply to it. `VOLUME` and the `MSTOP` fade-out also act separately from the mixer.

### CALL MTUNE(*reference frequency*)

Sets the master tuning. Specify the frequency of A4 as 430.0-450.0.
**It can be written as a real number** (`CALL MTUNE(442.5)`). Out of range gives `Illegal function call`.

It applies to all channels of all devices. The ADPCM playback rate moves with it.

- **`MINIT` returns it to 440.0.** To change it within a song, put it after `MINIT`
- The pitch actually played is **rounded to steps of 1/64 semitone** (1.5625 cents, about 0.4Hz at A4). This is because the tuning table is built in those steps
- It is an additive term independent of pitch bend (`P` `@P`) and portamento, and they add together

### CALL MUSIC / CALL AUDIO / CALL OPM / CALL MIDI

Switches page 1 to MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 / MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite / OPM BASIC Extension / MIDI Play BASIC Extension. The arguments are interpreted by each BASIC extension, so you can write them in the destination's syntax, as in `CALL MUSIC(-1)`.

### CALL VOICE COPY(*parameter 1*, *parameter 2*)

Copies voice data (for the FM sound chips). Same function as the statement of the same name in MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2, and the voice data layout is also the same (32 bytes). Voices used on OPM tracks are made in the [OPM voice](#opm-voice) layout.

A parameter is `@`*n* (a voice number) or the name of a numeric array written without parentheses. Copies from the first parameter to the second parameter.

| Voice number | |
|---|---|
| 0-63 | Presets. **Read-only** |
| 128-191 | Voices made by the program. Both readable and writable |

It is an error when the array is smaller than 32 bytes, when a preset is specified as the destination, or when both are arrays.

```basic
10 DIM A%(15)
20 CALL VOICE COPY(@0, A%)     ' preset 0 to the array
30 A%(4) = 256                 ' raise the transpose by one semitone
40 CALL VOICE COPY(A%, @128)   ' register it as voice 128
50 CALL MTRK(0,0,"@128CDE")
```

### CALL WAVE COPY(*parameter 1*, *parameter 2*)

Copies waveform data (for the SCC). The parameters are the same as `VOICE COPY`; it copies data between waveform data (32 bytes) and array variables.

| Waveform number | |
|---|---|
| 0-15 | Presets. **Read-only** |
| 16-31 | Waveforms made by the program. Both readable and writable |

For the procedure to save the voices and waveforms you made to a file, see "[Saving and loading data](#saving-and-loading-data)".

### CALL ENV COPY(*parameter 1*, *parameter 2*)

Copies a [software envelope](#software-envelope--en) used by the SSGS and SCC. A parameter is `@`*n* (envelope number 1-31) or the name of a numeric array written without parentheses. Copies from the first parameter to the second parameter.

Copying between envelope numbers is also possible. `@0` (no envelope) and 32 or more are errors. Making both arrays is also an error.

The array holds the 4 bytes of the data (below) as they are. For an integer array that is 2 elements: the low byte of element 0 is AR, the high byte is DR, the low byte of element 1 is SL, and the high byte is RR. **When the array is larger than 2 elements, only the first 4 bytes are used and the rest is not touched. Fewer than 2 elements is an error.**

| Byte | Parameter | Range |
|--:|---|---|
| 0 | AR (attack rate) | 0-32 |
| 1 | DR (decay rate) | 0-32 |
| 2 | SL (sustain level) | 0-15 |
| 3 | RR (release rate) | 0-32 |

Value ranges are not checked. A rate beyond the range plays as 32, and a level as 15.

**Definitions are cleared by `CALL MINIT`** (all become 0). How it sounds when `@E`*n* selects a number that has not been defined is not guaranteed.

```basic
10 DIM A%(1)
20 A%(0) = 16 + 20 * 256      ' AR=16, DR=20
30 A%(1) = 8 + 10 * 256       ' SL=8, RR=10
40 CALL ENV COPY(A%, @1)      ' register it as envelope 1
50 CALL MTRK(0,0,"@E1V15CDE")
```

### CALL SET PCM *voice file*, *device*, *mode*, *parameter 1*, *parameter 2*[, *sampling frequency*][, *channel*]

Initializes an ADPCM voice file. Same function as the statement of the same name in MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite.

*voice file number* is 0-63, and ties the number that later PCM-related statements refer to to the actual data.

*device number* specifies where the voice file is stored (the storage). Note that it is not the same thing as the Y8960 device numbers. The meanings of *parameter 1* and *parameter 2* change with the specified device.

| Device number | Device name | Mode | Parameter 1 | Parameter 2 |
|--:|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | External RAM | 0 | - | Length |
| 4 | Main RAM | 0 | Array name | - |
| 5 | VRAM | 0 | Address | Length |

Omit those marked `-`. The unit of length is 256 bytes. External RAM refers to the 256KB of ADPCM memory of the OPL2EX. Because this is the only ADPCM memory, there is no external RAM for the second channel (MSX-AUDIO device number 2), and there is no external ROM (1, 3) either.

**This statement does not move data.** It only ties a voice file number to the location of its contents; what actually carries the data is `CALL COPY PCM`.

| Device | How it is handled |
|---|---|
| External RAM | Allocates an area of *parameter 2* pages from the free space in ADPCM memory. **Only voice files in this location can be played from MML** — the sound chip can read only its own memory |
| Main RAM | The array variable itself is the contents. The length is determined by the size of the array, and any fraction under 256 bytes is discarded. **It remembers the name, not the address**, so it follows the array when variables are added and the array moves |
| VRAM | From the page of *parameter 1*, for *parameter 2* pages. A page is a VRAM address divided by 256: 0-511 (128KB) on MSX2 and later, 0-63 (16KB) on MSX1. An area that extends outside VRAM is an error |

**Areas are allocated by searching for free space from the start.** Reassigning the same number first releases the previous area. Specifying a length of 0 only releases that number. If there is not enough free space, it is an error. An array smaller than one page is also an error.

*mode* is fixed at 0 (ADPCM). There is no MSX-AUDIO PCM mode.

The unit of *sampling frequency* is Hz, and the range is 1800-16000Hz. The initial value is 8000Hz.
The pitch that plays at the frequency given here is `O5 E`.

*channel number* is accepted but **has no effect.** Only channel 9 of the OPL2EX plays ADPCM memory, and which track plays it is decided by `MASSIGN`.

**ADPCM data is not included in sequence data.** `MSAVE` writes out voices and waveforms only, so if a song loaded with `MLOAD` uses ADPCM, the playing side must prepare voice files with the same numbers using `SET PCM` and `COPY PCM`.

Sequence data contains, for the voice files the song uses that are placed in ADPCM memory, a record of their location, length and sampling frequency. `MLOAD` does not use it. Keeping the contents of ADPCM memory consistent with this record is the responsibility of the user.

**`CALL MINIT` forgets all voice files.** The contents of ADPCM memory remain, so if you only need to renumber them, external RAM is enough.

```basic
10 CALL SET PCM(0,0,0,,64)     ' 16KB in ADPCM memory
20 CALL SET PCM(1,5,0,64,64)   ' 16KB from 4000H in VRAM
30 CALL COPY PCM(1,0)          ' from VRAM to where it can be played
```

### CALL COPY PCM(*source voice file number*, *destination voice file number*[, *offset 1*][, *length*][, *offset 2*])

Transfers ADPCM data between voice files. **This is the only way both into ADPCM memory and out of it.**

Copies *length* from *offset 1* of the *source* to *offset 2* of the *destination*. **The unit of both offsets and length is 256 bytes.**

When omitted, offsets are 0, and length is "the shorter of what remains in the source and in the destination".
A specified length that exceeds this is also cut down to the shorter one. An offset equal to or greater than the file length is an error.

A transfer does not change the length or location of the destination voice file.

**Transfers from ADPCM memory to ADPCM memory are not possible** (error). The sound chip has only one address counter, so it cannot read and write at the same time. Transfers to and from arrays and VRAM are possible in either direction. For the procedure to save ADPCM data to a file, see "[Saving and loading data](#saving-and-loading-data)".

```basic
10 CALL SET PCM(0,4,0,S%)      ' array S%
20 CALL SET PCM(1,0,0,,4)      ' 1KB in ADPCM memory
30 CALL COPY PCM(0,1)          ' from the array to ADPCM memory
40 CALL COPY PCM(1,0,2,1,0)    ' 1 page from the 2nd page to the start of the array
```

### CALL EXPORT PCM(*file name*, *mode*)

Writes the voice file settings and the contents of ADPCM memory to a disk file.

| Argument | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| File name | String | `[`*drive*`:]`*name*`[.`*extension*`]`. The name is up to 8 characters and the extension up to 3. No extension is added automatically |
| Mode | 1-3 | 1 voice file settings / 2 ADPCM memory / 3 both |

**The settings written out are only those of voice files placed in ADPCM memory.** They contain the number, location, length and sampling frequency. Voice files in array variables and VRAM have meaning only on that machine at that time, so they are not written out.

**ADPCM memory is written out from the start up to the last page reached by a voice file placed in ADPCM memory.** If none is placed there, there are no contents.

A file with the same name is replaced. A name containing wildcards (`*` `?`) or a name that is too long gives `Bad file name`, and insufficient free disk space gives `Disk full`.
**A machine without a disk gives `Illegal function call`.**

It can be executed during playback. While it is writing, notes on the ADPCM channel may drop out.

```basic
10 CALL EXPORT PCM("DRUMS.PCM",3)
```

### CALL IMPORT PCM(*file name*, *mode*)

Loads the voice file settings and the contents of ADPCM memory from a file written by `CALL EXPORT PCM`. The arguments are the same as `CALL EXPORT PCM`.

**Loading the settings replaces all voice file settings.** Numbers not in the file end up with no settings. The settings of voice files in array variables and VRAM are also cleared.

**Loading ADPCM memory overwrites as many pages as the file has, starting at page 0.** Anything beyond that remains as it is.

When the contents requested by the mode are not in the file (such as reading a settings-only file with 2), `Illegal function call`.

**When a sequence or `MPLAY` is playing, `Illegal function call`.** A paused sequence is fine.

| Situation | Error | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| The file does not exist | `File not found` | Nothing changes |
| The name is invalid | `Bad file name` | Nothing changes |
| Not a file written by `CALL EXPORT PCM` | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |
| A setting value is out of range (number, location, sampling frequency) | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |
| The file is cut off partway | `Illegal function call` | Whatever could be read has been rewritten |
| A machine without a disk | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |

```basic
10 CALL IMPORT PCM("DRUMS.PCM",3)
20 CALL MSTART(&B0001)
```

#### File format

**The byte-level layout is in [`pcmfile.md`](pcmfile.md).** You need it when creating the same file on a PC, or when extracting the contents from an exported file.

### CALL SAVE PCM(*file name*, *voice file number*)

Writes a single voice file to a disk file. The file format is the same as what `CALL SAVE PCM` of the MSX-AUDIO BASIC extension writes.

| Argument | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| File name | String | Same as `CALL EXPORT PCM` |
| Voice file number | 0-63 | |

**What is written out is the contents of the voice file, its length and its sampling frequency.** The location may be any of ADPCM memory, array variables or VRAM. The location is not stored in the file.

A number not set with `CALL SET PCM` gives `Illegal function call`. File names and disks behave the same as `CALL EXPORT PCM` — a file with the same name is replaced, an invalid name gives `Bad file name`, insufficient free space gives `Disk full`, and a machine without a disk gives `Illegal function call`.

It can be executed during playback.

```basic
10 CALL SAVE PCM("DRUM1.PCM",1)
```

### CALL LOAD PCM(*file name*, *voice file number*)

Loads a file written by `CALL SAVE PCM` into a single voice file. Files written by `CALL SAVE PCM` of the MSX-AUDIO BASIC extension can also be read. The arguments are the same as `CALL SAVE PCM`.

**Prepare the voice file with `CALL SET PCM` first.** Loading does not change the location or the length. The sampling frequency becomes the one in the file.

**How much is loaded depends on the location.**

| Location | Amount loaded | When the file's contents are shorter than the recorded length |
|---|---|---|
| ADPCM memory, VRAM | The shorter of the voice file's length and the length recorded in the file | `Input past end` |
| Array variable | Up to the end of the file. If longer than the array, it is cut at the size of the array | Not an error. The rest of the array stays as it is |

**Files in MSX-AUDIO PCM mode cannot be read.** The Y8960 can only play ADPCM.

It can be executed during playback.

| Situation | Error | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| The file does not exist | `File not found` | Nothing changes |
| The name is invalid | `Bad file name` | Nothing changes |
| Not a file written by `CALL SAVE PCM` | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |
| A PCM mode file | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |
| The sampling frequency is outside 1800-16000Hz | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |
| A number that has not been set | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |
| The contents fall short of the recorded length (ADPCM memory, VRAM) | `Input past end` | The pages that could be read have been rewritten. The sampling frequency does not change |
| A machine without a disk | `Illegal function call` | Nothing changes |

```basic
10 CALL SET PCM(1,0,0,,16)
20 CALL LOAD PCM("DRUM1.PCM",1)
```

#### File format

**The byte-level layout is in "Single voice file" in [`pcmfile.md`](pcmfile.md).**

## Saving and loading data

The data that can be read from and written to files directly is sequence data (storage 2 of `CALL MSAVE` `CALL MLOAD`) and ADPCM data (`CALL SAVE PCM` `CALL LOAD PCM` `CALL EXPORT PCM` `CALL IMPORT PCM`). FM voices and SCC waveforms are **first copied to an array variable, and moved to and from files with MSX-BASIC's own features.** Sequence data can also be moved the same way, through an array variable or VRAM.

| Data | To array variable/VRAM | From array variable/VRAM | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sequence data | `CALL MSAVE` | `CALL MLOAD` | Array variable, VRAM |
| FM voice | `CALL VOICE COPY(@`*n*`, `*array*`)` | `CALL VOICE COPY(`*array*`, @`*n*`)` | Array variable |
| SCC waveform | `CALL WAVE COPY(@`*n*`, `*array*`)` | `CALL WAVE COPY(`*array*`, @`*n*`)` | Array variable |
| ADPCM data | `CALL COPY PCM` | `CALL COPY PCM` | Array variable, VRAM (the location is set with `CALL SET PCM`) |

Moving to and from files is the same for every kind of data. All the examples below are run after `CALL MINIT` has been done.

| Location | To file | From file |
|---|---|---|
| Array variable | `COPY A% TO "SONG.SEQ"` | `COPY "SONG.SEQ" TO A%` |
| VRAM | `BSAVE "SONG.VRM",`*start*`,`*end*`,S` | `BLOAD "SONG.VRM",S` |

**`COPY` between array variables and files exists only in the BASIC of MSX2 and later.** On MSX1, move the contents of array variables with `BSAVE` and `BLOAD` ("[Using array variables on MSX1](#using-array-variables-on-msx1)").
The examples that use VRAM (the `S` option of `BSAVE` / `BLOAD`) work as they are on MSX1 too.

**When loading into an array variable, `DIM` it first.** If the array is larger than the file, it is filled from the start and the rest stays as it is. **If it is smaller, the data is cut off partway without an error**, so make it the same size as when it was saved, or larger.

**Use `&H2000`-`&H3FFF` of VRAM, and do it while in `SCREEN 0`.** The `S` option of `BSAVE` and `BLOAD` does not handle addresses from `&H4000` up correctly. Below `&H2000` is used by the `SCREEN 0` display. The usable size is 8KB.

### Sequence data

**To just play a song, saving the sequence data alone is enough.** The FM voices and SCC waveforms it uses are included in the sequence data (`CALL MSAVE`). ADPCM data is not included, so if it is used, save it separately (below).

**To exchange directly with a disk file, use storage 2 of `CALL MSAVE` and `CALL MLOAD`.** It goes through neither an array variable nor VRAM. The following are the procedures that go through an array variable or VRAM.

Save to an array variable.

```basic
10 CALL MSIZE(0,S)
20 DIM A%(S/2)
30 CALL MSAVE(0,0,A%)
40 COPY A% TO "SONG.SEQ"
```

Load and play. The *size* for `CALL MLOAD` does not have to be exactly the size of the data; passing the size of the array (number of elements × 2 bytes) is enough.

```basic
10 DIM A%(1023)                 ' songs up to 2048 bytes
20 COPY "SONG.SEQ" TO A%
30 CALL MLOAD(0,0,A%,2048)
40 CALL MSTART(&B0001)
```

Save to VRAM.

```basic
10 CALL MSIZE(0,S)
20 CALL MSAVE(0,1,&H2000)
30 BSAVE "SONG.VRM",&H2000,&H2000+S-1,S
```

Load and play. No array variable is used, so no BASIC memory is used.

```basic
10 BLOAD "SONG.VRM",S
20 CALL MLOAD(0,1,&H2000,8192)
30 CALL MSTART(&B0001)
```

### FM voices and SCC waveforms

**`CALL MINIT` discards the voices (128-191) and waveforms (16-31) you made.**
To keep using them, save them and register them again after `CALL MINIT`. Each one is 32 bytes and goes through an array one at a time.

Save.

```basic
10 DIM V%(15),W%(15)
20 CALL VOICE COPY(@128,V%)
30 CALL WAVE COPY(@16,W%)
40 COPY V% TO "VOICE128.DAT"
50 COPY W% TO "WAVE16.DAT"
```

Load and register.

```basic
10 DIM V%(15),W%(15)
20 COPY "VOICE128.DAT" TO V%
30 COPY "WAVE16.DAT" TO W%
40 CALL VOICE COPY(V%,@128)
50 CALL WAVE COPY(W%,@16)
```

### ADPCM data

**For one voice file at a time, `CALL SAVE PCM` and `CALL LOAD PCM`** exchange directly with a disk file.

To go through an array variable, copy to an array variable or VRAM with `CALL COPY PCM`, then save.
The unit of length in `CALL SET PCM` is 256 bytes.

Save voice file 1 in ADPCM memory (16 pages = 4KB) to an array variable.

```basic
10 DIM P%(2047)                 ' 4096 bytes
20 CALL SET PCM(0,4,0,P%)
30 CALL COPY PCM(1,0)
40 COPY P% TO "VOICE1.PCM"
```

Load it and make it voice file 1 in ADPCM memory.

```basic
10 DIM P%(2047)
20 COPY "VOICE1.PCM" TO P%
30 CALL SET PCM(0,4,0,P%)
40 CALL SET PCM(1,0,0,,16)
50 CALL COPY PCM(0,1)
```

Array variables are placed in BASIC memory, so they are not suited to large data.

**To move everything together with the voice file settings, use `CALL EXPORT PCM` and `CALL IMPORT PCM`.**
They exchange directly with a disk file, so they go through neither an array variable nor VRAM. The number, location, length and sampling frequency of the voice files placed in ADPCM memory, and the contents of ADPCM memory, go into one file.

Save the voice files in ADPCM memory together with their settings.

```basic
10 CALL EXPORT PCM("PCMBANK.PCM",3)
```

Load. The existing voice file settings are replaced by the settings in the file.

```basic
10 CALL IMPORT PCM("PCMBANK.PCM",3)
```

### Using array variables on MSX1

Instead of `COPY`, save the memory where the array elements are laid out with `BSAVE`, and load it with `BLOAD`. Replace the `COPY` lines in the examples above with this form. It works the same way on MSX2 and later.

Save sequence data. *end* is the address of the last element +1 (an integer element is 2 bytes).

```basic
10 CALL MSIZE(0,S)
20 DIM A%(S/2)
30 CALL MSAVE(0,0,A%)
40 BSAVE "SONG.SEQ",VARPTR(A%(0)),VARPTR(A%(S/2))+1
```

Load and play. `BLOAD` tries to load to the address it was saved from, so pass the difference from the current array address as the offset. The address at save time is in bytes 2-3 of the first 7 bytes of the file (the header that `BSAVE` writes).

```basic
10 DIM A%(1023)
20 OPEN "SONG.SEQ" AS #1 LEN=7
30 FIELD #1,7 AS H$
40 GET #1,1
50 T=CVI(MID$(H$,2,2))
60 CLOSE #1
70 BLOAD "SONG.SEQ",VARPTR(A%(0))-T
80 CALL MLOAD(0,0,A%,2048)
90 CALL MSTART(&B0001)
```

**Do not make the array you load into smaller than it was at save time.** Unlike `COPY`, `BLOAD` writes the full length of the file, so whatever does not fit is written into the memory after the array.

## MML

The MML commands are the same as [MsxMusicBasicExtension](../../msx-music/en/basic-reference.md).
The following loop commands are added. They can be used only in tracks registered with `MTRK`, not with `MPLAY`.

| Command | Function |
|---|---|
| `\|:` | Loop start point. **Nesting up to 4 levels** |
| `:\|`*n* | Loop end point. *n* sets the loop count. When omitted, 1. 0 means an infinite loop |
| `[`*n* | Opens a block that is played only on the *n*th time through the loop. *n* **cannot be omitted** |
| `]` | Closes the block. **Can be omitted** (below) |
| `(DC)` | Da capo. Returns to the beginning |
| `(DS)`*n* | Dal segno. Jumps to the segno. *n* is the segno number (**0-3**). When omitted, 0. Ignored if there is no matching segno |
| `(*)`*n* | Segno. *n* is the segno number (**0-3**). When omitted, 0 |
| `(TC)`*n* | To Coda. Jumps to the coda when this point is reached for the *n*th time. *n* is **1-255**; when omitted, 2. Ignored if there is no matching coda |
| `(CODA)` | Coda. The jump target of `(TC)` |
| `(FINE)`*n* | Fine. Ends the sequence when this point is reached for the *n*th time. *n* is **1-255**; when omitted, 2 |

These **can be used the same way in the MML for rhythm sounds.**

#### `O`*n*

**Octaves are 0-9.** MsxMusicBasicExtension uses 1-8. `<` stops at `O0` and `>` stops at `O9`; they do not move beyond that. It is not an error.

Every octave can be written, but not every sound chip can produce all of them. How notes outside the range a sound chip can produce will sound is not guaranteed ([Pitches that cannot be produced](#pitches-that-cannot-be-produced)).

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"O0C")     ' accepted
CALL MTRK(0,0,"O0<C")    ' < does not move; O0C
CALL MTRK(0,0,"O10C")    ' Illegal function call
```

#### `N`*n*

**Note numbers are 0-127.** MsxMusicBasicExtension uses 0-96. The counting is the same: `N0` is `O1C` and `N36` is `O4C`. The notes of `O0` cannot be written with `N`.

**`N0` plays `O1C` on every sound chip.** It is not a rest.

#### `C-` and `B+`

**Only that one note moves to the adjacent octave.** `O4C-` sounds at the same pitch as `O3B`, and `O4B+` at the same pitch as `O5C`; the next note is again played in `O4`. This differs from MsxMusicBasicExtension, which wraps around within the same octave (`O4C-` is `O4B`).

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"O4C-C")   ' O3B, then O4C
CALL MTRK(0,0,"O4B+B")   ' O5C, then O4B
```

#### `&` (tie / legato)

**Joins** the notes before and after it. If they are the same note, it is a tie; if they are different notes, it is a legato (only the pitch changes, without re-sounding, so the envelope does not restart).

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"O4C4&C4")     ' sounds as a half note
CALL MTRK(0,0,"O4C4&E4")     ' moves from C to E without re-sounding
```

**A note before `&` sounds for its full length regardless of `Q`.** `Q` applies only to the last note, and to that note's own length, not to the total of the joined lengths, so even for the same length, where the sound is cut depends on how the notes are joined.

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"Q4O4C4&E4")   ' C sounds the full quarter note, E is cut at half
CALL MTRK(0,0,"Q4O4A4")      ' sounds for an eighth note, then is cut
CALL MTRK(0,0,"Q4O4A8&A8")   ' sounds for an eighth plus a sixteenth note, then is cut
```

Write `&` immediately after the note. If another command is placed in between, as in `C4V10&E4`, `C` is cut partway according to `Q`, and `E` is sounded again normally.

#### Blocks (first and second endings)

A block starts with `[`*n* and **ends at `]`, at the next `[`, or at the loop end `:|`.** Whether to write `]` depends on what you want to place after the block.

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"|:ABC[1D[2E:|2")        ' 1st time ABC D / 2nd time ABC E
CALL MTRK(0,0,"|:ABC[1D][2E]F:|2")     ' 1st time ABC D F / 2nd time ABC E F
```

Consecutive blocks form one **group**. A group ends when a block ends and what follows is not `[`.

- **If there is no block corresponding to the loop count, the last block of the group is played.** It is not an error
- A loop may contain two or more groups. The numbers are counted within each group

#### Limits

| | |
|---|---|
| Nesting of `\|:` | 4 levels |
| Segno number of `(*)`*n* and `(DS)`*n* | 0-3 |
| Total of `(TC)` and `(FINE)` in one track | 8 |
| Arrival count of `(TC)`*n* and `(FINE)`*n* | 1-255 |

**Exceeding these is `Illegal function call`.** Silently truncating them would make what plays a different piece from what was written.

#### Fine points

- **`(TC)` and `(CODA)`, and `(DS)` and `(*)`, may be written in separate `MTRK` calls.** Within the same track, they pair up with one another whichever `MTRK` they were written in. `(TC)` jumps to the track's `(CODA)`, whether that comes before it or is written later. `(DS)`*n* jumps to the last of the `(*)`*n* with the same number written before it. There is one `(CODA)` per track; a second one is `Illegal function call` even in a separate `MTRK`
- **Close everything within a single `MTRK`.** If an `MTRK` ends with `|:` still open, or with a block group still open, it is `Illegal function call`. The same as tuplet `{ }`
- **`|:` cannot be placed inside a block.** Placing it there is `Illegal function call`. It can be placed once the block group has been closed (`|:A[1B]C|:D:|2:|2` is accepted)
- **Case does not matter.** `(DC)` and `(dc)` are the same
- **Spaces may be inserted in the middle of a symbol.** `\| :` and `( D C )` are also accepted. MML skips spaces everywhere
- **An infinite loop with no notes or rests ends that track there.** If you write a loop that takes no time, such as `|::|0`, `MTRK` accepts it, but playback ends that track once it has read 256 events. Otherwise the machine would stop responding
- **When a pass ends at `(DC)` or `(FINE)`, the sound still playing is stopped by the first command of the next pass.** Both notes and rests start by stopping the sound that is playing, so a track that starts with either leaves no sound behind. **Only `@W`*n* does not stop the sound, so a track whose pass starts with `@W`*n* enters the next pass still holding the last note of the previous pass.** When the repeats are used up and playback ends, the sound stops on every track

### Note lengths and tuplets

Note lengths go up to **96**. This applies to `Ln` `Rn` `@Wn` `{ }`*n* and to every length written directly on a note.

**An `R` with its length omitted takes the length of `L`*n*.** It is read the same way as a note: inside `{ }`*n* it takes its share, if a length is written it has that length, and a dot applies in every case. `L8R` is an eighth rest.
In the extension this is taken from, `R` is a quarter rest regardless of `L`, so this point differs.

Notes inside `{ }`*n* sound with the length of an *n*th note divided by the number of notes. `{CDE}4` lines up C D E, each one third of a quarter note. If *n* is omitted, the value of `Ln` is used.

- **A note with its own length written keeps that length.** The remaining notes receive the shares. In `{C8DE}4`, C is an eighth note, and D and E are each one third of a quarter note
- **If the number of notes × *n* exceeds 96, it is `Illegal function call`.** `{CDE}32` is accepted; `{CDE}33` is not
- **`{ }` cannot be nested**
- **Pair `{` and `}` within the same `MTRK`**
- **Only notes, `Rn` and `Nn` are counted.** `&` and `@Wn` take time but are not counted, so the tuplet becomes longer than an *n*th note by that amount

### Variable references

`=`*x*`;` can be used **anywhere a number can be written**. `O=A;C` sets the octave to the value of variable A and then plays C.

`X`*x*`;` switches to the MML stored in string variable *x* and continues reading from there. The length, volume and octave set before the switch remain in effect.

- **MML cannot be written after `X`*x*`;`.** Writing it is `Illegal function call`
- **Up to 8 strings can be chained with `X`*x*`;`.** Because a variable that points to itself would never end
- **Both take only a variable name.** Expressions and arrays cannot be written
- The name is closed with `;`. If it is not closed, it is `Illegal function call`

### Pitches that cannot be produced

Not every sound chip can produce all of `O0`-`O9`. **Going outside the range is not an error either, but how it sounds is not guaranteed.** The current behavior is as follows.

| Sound chip | What cannot be produced | Current behavior |
|---|---|---|
| OPLLEX / OPL2EX | From `G` of `O8` upward (the chip's limit is about 6.2kHz) | All play the highest note that can be produced |
| OPLLEX / OPL2EX | `C` to `F+` of `O0` | Pitch accuracy drops slightly. Going further down with pitch bend makes it coarser, and eventually silent |
| SSGS / SCC | From `G+` of `O0` downward | All play the lowest note that can be produced (slightly lower than `O0A`) |
| SSGS / SCC | `O9` | The pitch is produced but coarse; some adjacent notes come out at the same pitch |
| OPM | From `C+` of `O8` upward | All play the highest note that can be produced (slightly below `C+` of `O8`) |
| OPM | `C` of `O0` | The lowest note that can be produced (`C+` of `O0`) |

The same applies when pitch bend or portamento goes outside the range.

**`<` and `>` inside a loop can move the octave outside `O0`-`O9` as passes accumulate.** `MTRK` stops them only when reading in the order written; it does not stop the accumulation across passes. Notes that go outside the range are not guaranteed.

### Differences between sound chips

Which commands take effect on which sound chips follows "MML and each sound chip" in MsxMusicBasicExtension. The differences on Y8960 are as follows.

| Command | Meaning on Y8960 |
|---|---|
| `@`*n* | The meaning differs by sound chip. On the FM sound chips (OPLLEX, OPL2EX, OPM) it is the voice number (presets 0-63, OPLLEX built-in voices 65-127, voices made with `VOICE COPY` 128-191; below). On SCC it is the **waveform number 0-31** (0-15 are presets, 16-31 are waveforms made with `WAVE COPY`). On SSGS it is the **mixer and envelope setting** (below) |
| `{ }`*n* | **Usable on all sound chips.** In MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2 and MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite it can be used only on FM sound chips |
| `@E`*n* | **Software envelope for SSGS and SCC** (below). Ignored on other sound chips |
| `@V`*n* | **1 is 0.75 dB.** `@V127` is the loudest, and each step down by 1 is 0.75 dB quieter. `V`*n* is the same as `@V`(4*n*+67), and one step of `V` is 3 dB. On sound chips that hold volume in only 4 bits (the OPLLEX FM sound, SCC, rhythm sounds), 4 of `@V` corresponds to one step of `V` (below, "`V` and `@V`"). **On SSGS it is separate from `V`: a linear volume per channel** (below) |
| `V`*n* `@V`*n* | On SCC, the 0-15 volume is **converted to an SCC volume through a table before it is written** (below). On SSGS, `V` is a 4-bit volume and `@V` is the per-channel **linear volume register** (0-128); they take effect separately (below, "`V` and `@V`") |
| `i`*n* | **Panning**. Effective on all sound chips (below). 1-255 |
| `@G`*n* | **Whether to convert the SCC volume through the table**. `@G1` converts and `@G0` does not (below). Ignored on other sound chips |

#### `V` and `@V`

**`@V` is for sound chips that hold volume more finely than 4 bits.** These are the OPL2EX FM sound and ADPCM, and OPM; 1 of `@V` takes effect directly as 0.75 dB (the OPL2EX FM sound can be lowered by up to 47.25 dB, OPM by up to 95.25 dB).

**On SSGS, `@V` is a volume separate from `V`.** SSGS has a linear volume register per channel (0-128; 128 passes the signal through unchanged), and `@V`*n* writes that value. Only on SSGS can `@V` be written up to 128. 1 is 1/128, and the steps are not evenly spaced in dB. `V` is the 4-bit volume as usual, and `VOLUME`, the `MSTOP` fade-out and `MMUTE` also act on it. Changing `@V` does not change `V`, and changing `V` does not change `@V`. The actual volume is the product of the two. `@V` returns to 128 each time the piece repeats.

On sound chips that hold volume in only 4 bits, the 16 steps of `V` are output as they are. `@V`*n* sounds at the step obtained by subtracting (127 − *n*) ÷ 4 (rounded down) from 15, and at 0 if that falls below 0. No differences finer than `V` are produced.

#### SCC volume

The SCC volume register is proportional to amplitude, so writing the same values as for SSGS makes low volumes sound loud. Therefore `V`*n* and the software envelope values are converted through the following table before they are written.

| `V` | 0 | 1-7 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11 | 12 | 13 | 14 | 15 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SCC volume | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 15 |

**`V1` to `V7` sound at the same volume.** `@V`*n* looks up the table using the step obtained in the "`V` and `@V`" section as `V`. Values written directly to registers with `Y` do not go through the table.

**`@G0` bypasses the table.** `V`*n* and the software envelope values (0-15) are written as the SCC volume as they are. This is for playing MML whose volumes were written as SCC volume register values with the same balance. `@G1` returns to converting through the table.

- A track starts at `@G1`, and returns to `@G1` each time the piece repeats
- Switching in the middle of a note changes the volume of the sounding note on the spot
- `@G2` and above are an error
- Volume lowered by `CALL VOLUME`, the `MSTOP` fade-out or `MMUTE` is subtracted from `V` by the same amount even with `@G0`. Because the result does not go through the table, the same reduction sounds different from a `@G1` track in how much quieter it gets

#### `@`*n* on the FM sound chips

| *n* | OPLLEX | OPL2EX | OPM |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-63 | Preset | Preset | OPM preset (below) |
| 64 | Error | Error | Error |
| 65-127 | Built-in voice of the chip. bit5-4 of *n*−64 is the voice bank (0-3), bit3-0 is the voice number within the bank (1-15; 0 is the chip's user voice). **List below** | Ignored (the previous voice remains) | Ignored (the previous voice remains) |
| 128-191 | Voice made with `VOICE COPY` | Voice made with `VOICE COPY` | Voice made with `VOICE COPY`, read as [OPM voice data](#opm-voice) |

**On OPLLEX, presets and voices you make are played using the chip's user voice.**
Each OPLLEX instance has only one user voice, so if two channels of the same OPLLEX play different presets at the same time, both sound with the voice selected later. Built-in voices (65-127) can be selected per channel.

**Notes before any `@`*n* is written sound with `@0`.**
On the ADPCM channel this is voice file 0. Each time the piece repeats, it starts again from this voice. **It is treated the same as writing `@0`**, so on OPLLEX, at the first note, the track sets the chip's user voice to `@0`. If another channel of the same OPLLEX has selected a preset, that channel also ends up sounding with `@0`.

#### OPLLEX built-in voices

Each bank has 15 voices. The names are those in each chip's voice table; the same name in a different bank is a different voice.

| Bank | Chip | `@`*n* |
|--:|---|---|
| 0 | OPLL (YM2413 equivalent) | `@65`-`@79` |
| 1 | OPLL-X (YM2423 equivalent) | `@81`-`@95` |
| 2 | OPLL-P (YMF281 equivalent) | `@97`-`@111` |
| 3 | VRC7 (DS1001 equivalent) | `@113`-`@127` |

| `@`*n* | Bank 0 (OPLL) | `@`*n* | Bank 1 (OPLL-X) |
|--:|---|--:|---|
| 65 | Violin | 81 | Strings |
| 66 | Guitar | 82 | Guitar |
| 67 | Piano | 83 | Electric Guitar |
| 68 | Flute | 84 | Electric Piano 2 |
| 69 | Clarinet | 85 | Flute |
| 70 | Oboe | 86 | Marimba |
| 71 | Trumpet | 87 | Trumpet |
| 72 | Organ | 88 | Harmonica |
| 73 | Horn | 89 | Tuba |
| 74 | Synthesizer | 90 | Synth Brass 2 |
| 75 | Harpsichord | 91 | Short Saw |
| 76 | Vibraphone | 92 | Vibraphone |
| 77 | Synthesizer Bass | 93 | Electric Guitar 2 |
| 78 | Acoustic Bass | 94 | Synth Bass 2 |
| 79 | Electric Guitar | 95 | Sitar |

| `@`*n* | Bank 2 (OPLL-P) | `@`*n* | Bank 3 (VRC7) |
|--:|---|--:|---|
| 97 | Clarinet | 113 | Buzzy Bell |
| 98 | Synth Bass | 114 | Guitar |
| 99 | Piano | 115 | Wurly |
| 100 | Flute | 116 | Flute |
| 101 | Square Wave | 117 | Clarinet |
| 102 | Space Oboe | 118 | Synth |
| 103 | Trumpet | 119 | Trumpet |
| 104 | Wow Bell | 120 | Organ |
| 105 | Electric Guitar | 121 | Bells |
| 106 | Vibes | 122 | Vibes |
| 107 | Bass | 123 | Vibraphone |
| 108 | Vibraphone | 124 | Tutti |
| 109 | Vibrato Bell | 125 | Fretless |
| 110 | Click Sine | 126 | Synth Bass |
| 111 | Noise and Tone | 127 | Sweep |

**No bank has voice number 0.** `@80` `@96` `@112` select that bank and then play the chip's user voice: the same single one used by presets and by voices made with `VOICE COPY`, which other channels of the same OPLLEX overwrite. `@64` is `Illegal function call`.

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"@113O4CDE")   ' plays with the VRC7 Buzzy Bell
```

#### OPM voices

**All 64 OPM presets are the same voice** (a single sine wave). They are separate from the OPLLEX and OPL2EX presets and cannot be read out with `VOICE COPY` (`@0`-`@63` in `VOICE COPY` are the OPLLEX and OPL2EX presets).

**128-191 are numbers shared by the three FM sound chips.** The track's sound chip determines how the contents are read; on an OPM track they are read as [OPM voice data](#opm-voice). If the same number is used on OPLLEX and on OPM, one of them sounds broken.

**Noise sounds only on channel 7.** The noise bit of the voice data is written to the chip each time a voice is selected on channel 7. The noise frequency is written with `Y` into bit4-0 of `0FH`.

**The LFO is written with `Y`** (`18H` `19H` `1BH`). `CALL MINIT` stops it.

#### `@`*n* on the SSGS

SSGS has no voices, so `@`*n* specifies, together, the channel's **tone/noise output selection and hardware envelope selection**.

| Bit | Content |
|---|---|
| bit4-0 | The value written as is to the amplitude register (R8-R10). bit4 = 1 selects the hardware envelope; bit3-0 is the volume |
| bit5 | Tone. **Sounds when 0** |
| bit6 | Noise. **Sounds when 1** (the opposite of bit5) |

**When bit4 is 0, bit3-0 is not written.** When the hardware envelope is not used, the volume is held by `V`, so `@`*n* does not overwrite it.

| `@`*n* | Content |
|---|---|
| `@0` | Tone only (initial state) |
| `@64` | Tone + noise |
| `@96` | Noise only |
| `@32` | Neither sounds. **A DC level may be output** (a property of the SSG mixer; whether the Y8960's SSG behaves the same is unconfirmed) |
| `@16`+*v* | Hardware envelope, volume *v* (0-15) |

The selection takes effect per channel. The settings of the other channels of the same SSGS do not change.

#### Panning — `i`*n*

SSGS, OPLLEX, OPL2EX and SCC have a panpot for each channel. `i`*n* sets it. The value is the chip's register value as is. On OPL2EX it also applies to the ADPCM channel (CH9).

**OPM can only turn the left and right outputs on or off.** `i`*n* is rounded as follows.

| *n* | OPM |
|---|---|
| 1-64 | Left only |
| 65-191 | Both |
| 192-255 | Right only |

| *n* | Panning |
|---|---|
| 1 | Far left |
| 128 | Center |
| 255 | Far right |

In between is power panning; at the center, both left and right are 1/√2 (−3 dB).

**How `i0` sounds is not guaranteed.** 0 is a value the cartridge specification does not define, and it is written to the register as is (currently it sounds at the far left, the same as 1).

**`CALL MINIT` sets all channels to 128 (center).** On OPM, both outputs are turned on. Even if a previously running program left the panning to one side, a piece that does not write `i` sounds at the center.

**Rhythm sounds play at the panning of channels 6-8** (the bass drum on 6, the hi-hat and snare on 7, the tom and cymbal on 8). The same on both OPLLEX and OPL2EX. `i`*n* written in a track on the rhythm channel (CH10) moves those three together. To set instruments separately, write the registers with `Y` (`56H`-`58H` on OPLLEX, `FCH`-`FEH` on OPL2EX).

`i`*n* consumes no time. `s`*n* (envelope shape) and `m`*n* (envelope period) are not an error when written in a track assigned to anything other than SSGS, and do nothing. This is so that a score written for one sound chip does not stop when played on another.

#### Software envelope — `@E`*n*

Moves the volume of SSGS and SCC over time, for each note. It is the same envelope as in MuSICA; the *n* of `@E`*n* is a number (1-31) defined with `CALL ENV COPY`.
**`@E0` means no envelope**, and the volume stays at `V`. A track starts at `@E0`, and returns to `@E0` each time the piece repeats. 32 and above are an error.

Writing it in a track for FM, ADPCM or rhythm sounds is not an error, and does nothing.

**Behavior.** The value underlying the volume (0-15) moves as follows.

1. **Attack** — starts from 0 at key-on and rises to 15 at the AR rate
2. **Decay** — on reaching 15, falls at the DR rate, and stops at SL once it goes below SL
3. **Sustain** — stays at SL until key-off
4. **Release** — at key-off, falls from the value at that moment to 0 at the RR rate

**Rates are counted in frames of 1/60 second.** This is independent of the `CALL MINIT` resolution, and the same on PAL machines. The correspondence between the values of AR, DR and RR and the rates is as follows; larger values are faster. **0 does not mean "does not move"; it is the slowest.**

| Value | Frames | Change | Value | Frames | Change | Value | Frames | Change |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 15 | 1 | 11 | 5 | 2 | 22 | 1 | 3 |
| 1 | 12 | 1 | 12 | 2 | 1 | 23 | 2 | 7 |
| 2 | 10 | 1 | 13 | 5 | 3 | 24 | 1 | 4 |
| 3 | 9 | 1 | 14 | 3 | 2 | 25 | 1 | 5 |
| 4 | 8 | 1 | 15 | 4 | 3 | 26 | 1 | 6 |
| 5 | 7 | 1 | 16 | 1 | 1 | 27 | 1 | 7 |
| 6 | 6 | 1 | 17 | 3 | 4 | 28 | 1 | 8 |
| 7 | 5 | 1 | 18 | 2 | 3 | 29 | 1 | 9 |
| 8 | 4 | 1 | 19 | 3 | 5 | 30 | 1 | 10 |
| 9 | 7 | 2 | 20 | 1 | 2 | 31 | 1 | 12 |
| 10 | 3 | 1 | 21 | 2 | 5 | 32 | 1 | 15 |

The value moves by "Change" every "Frames" frames. For example, 16 moves by 1 every frame, and 0 moves by 1 every 15 frames. **The instants of key-on and key-off are the first frame of the attack and of the release respectively** (the same as MuSICA): with 16, the value becomes 1 at the instant of key-on. If key-off happens again during the release (such as a rest following a note cut by the gate), the release is counted again from the value at that moment.

**`V` works by subtraction.** The actual volume is "envelope value − (15 − `V`)", and 0 if that falls below 0. With `V15` the envelope value comes out as is. When `V` is small, the first (15 − `V`) frames of the attack are silent, and then the volume rises from 1 to `V`. What sounds during sustain is SL − (15 − `V`). Volume lowered by `@V`, `CALL VOLUME`, the `MSTOP` fade-out or `MMUTE` works the same way.

**Ties and legato do not go back to the attack.** Notes joined with `&` or with `~` without a number sound as a continuation of the previous note's envelope. Any other note restarts the attack from 0 at each key-on.

**Reselecting in the middle of a note.** Selecting `@E`*n* from no envelope during key-on starts from the attack on the spot. During key-off, it starts from the next key-on. Changing from one envelope to another continues from the stage and value at that moment, at the new rates. Selecting `@E0` returns to the `V` volume on the spot.

**Stopping.** With an `MSTOP` without fade-out and with `MPAUSE`, as on FM, **the release plays before the sound disappears.** When a channel is taken away by `MASSIGN` or `MFREE`, the sound disappears on the spot without waiting for the release.

**On SSGS, between the software envelope and the hardware envelope (`@16` and above), whichever is specified later takes effect.** `@E`*n* (1 or above) switches to the software envelope, and `@16` and above switch to the hardware envelope. The tone and noise selection is kept either way. `@0`-`@15` do not select the hardware envelope, so the software envelope continues.

**The sequence receives a copy of the envelope as it was at the time of `MTRK`.** Rewriting the same number with `ENV COPY` afterwards does not change how an already registered sequence sounds (running `MTRK` again copies the new definition). `MSAVE` writes this copy out together with the sequence.

### MML for ADPCM

A track assigned to the ADPCM channel (CH9) is **written the same way as for FM**. Only the meaning of the following commands differs.

| Command | Meaning on the ADPCM channel |
|---|---|
| `@`*n* | Selects the **voice file number 0-63** (made with `SET PCM`) |
| Notes, `N`*n* | Sound that voice file. **The pitch changes the playback rate** |
| `R`*n* | Stops the sound |
| `V`*n* `@V`*n* | ADPCM output level |

**`O5 E` is the pitch that plays at exactly the sampling frequency given with `SET PCM`**; each semitone away from it multiplies the playback rate by 2 to the power of 1/12. For pitches whose actual frequency would exceed 49716Hz, the rate is capped. The initial value of `SET PCM` is 8000Hz, so if nothing is specified, `O5 E` plays at 8000Hz.

`L`*n*, `O`*n*, `T`*n*, `Q`*n*, `>`, `<`, `.`, `=x;`, `Xx;`, `{ }`*n* are the same as for FM. Commands related to voices, pitch bend and envelopes are ignored.

### MML for rhythm sounds

A track assigned to the rhythm channel (CH10) is **written differently.**
To play several instruments at once in one track, list the instruments to play and write the length after them.

| Character | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `B` | Bass drum |
| `S` | Snare drum |
| `M` | Tom-tom |
| `C` | Cymbal |
| `H` | Hi-hat |
| `!` | Plays the preceding instrument at the accent volume |
| *n* | Plays the instruments listed so far, then waits for the length of an *n*th note. With `0`, does not wait (below) |
| `V`*n* | Sets the non-accented volume for all five instruments together. 0-15, default 8 |
| `@B`*n* `@S`*n* `@M`*n* `@C`*n* `@H`*n* | Sets the non-accented volume only for the instrument named by the letter after `@`. 0-15 |
| `@A`*n* | Accented volume. Common to all five instruments. 0-15, default 15 |
| `@V`*n* | Specifies the same thing as `V`, in 0-127. For how the step is obtained, see "`V` and `@V`" |

`T`*n*, `R`*n*, `@W`*n*, `Y`*r*`,`*d*`,`*m*, `=x;`, `Xx;`, `.` are the same as for FM.
**There is no `L`*n***, so write the length after every list of instruments.

```basic
CALL MASSIGN(0,0,1,10)
CALL MTRK(0,0,"T120V10@A3BSH8H8S!H8H8")
```

- Plays the bass, snare and hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note
- Plays the hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note
- Plays the snare with an accent together with the hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note
- Plays the hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note

Instruments decay each time they are struck, so **there is no way to write stopping a sound.** `Q`*n* has no effect either.

**For the volume of each instrument, whichever is written later takes effect.** `@B`*n* and the like change only that instrument, while `V`*n* and `@V`*n* change all five. So writing `V` overwrites any `@B`*n* and the like written before it. An instrument marked with `!` sounds at the `@A`*n* volume, whichever instrument it is.

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"V10@H6@B13BH8H8S!H8H8")
```

- Sets the hi-hat to 6, the bass drum to 13, and the other instruments to 10
- The accented snare sounds at 15, the default of `@A`

Like `V`, the volume of each instrument returns to its default (8 for all five) when the sequence starts playing ([Rhythm mode](#rhythm-mode)).

**Writing `0` as the length plays the instruments without taking time.** Follow it with `@W`*n* or an `R`*n* with a length to wait. Between playing and waiting, you can insert commands that take no time, such as `Y`.

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"B0@W8H8")
```

- Plays the bass drum and moves on without taking time
- Waits for an eighth note (up to this point, the same as `B8`)
- Plays the hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note

**You cannot play twice without advancing time.** After a length of 0, if nothing that advances time (`@W`*n*, or an `R`*n* with a length) is placed before the next instruments are played, it is `Illegal function call`. Playing first stops all the listed instruments and then plays them, so a second play at the same instant would stop the first at the very moment it is struck. Write instruments that play together in one list, as in `BH8`. `@W0` is also `Illegal function call`.

On OPLLEX and OPL2EX, **the same `V` gives the same volume.** OPL2EX does not have rhythm sounds in the chip, so on entering rhythm mode, rhythm voices are loaded into channels 6-8 ([Rhythm mode](#rhythm-mode)).

**`i`*n* can also be written.** The panning of the rhythm sounds (the three channels 6-8) moves together ([Panning](#panning--in)). The same on both OPLLEX and OPL2EX.

### Register writes with `Y`

`Y`*r*`,`*d* writes *d* to register *r* of the sound chip the track uses. It consumes no time, and any number of them can be lined up. **On every sound chip, the register numbers are the chip's own**, and the sound chip written to is determined by the device specified with `MASSIGN`.

| Sound chip | Accepted *r* | *d* |
|---|---|---|
| SSGS | `00H`-`0DH` (first set), `10H`-`1DH` (second set), channel volume `20H`-`22H` `24H`-`26H` (effective at 0-128), panning `28H`-`2AH` `2CH`-`2EH` | 0-255 |
| OPLLEX | `00H`-`07H`, `0EH`-`18H`, `20H`-`28H`, `30H`-`38H`, bank registers `40H`-`48H`, panning `50H`-`58H` | 0-255 |
| OPL2EX | `00H`-`FFH`. However, **`04H` cannot be written** (below). Panning is `F6H`-`FEH` (channels 0-8) and `FFH` (ADPCM) | 0-255 |
| SCC | `00H`-`FFH`. An offset from the start of the register window, counted the same way as `SQSCCW`. **Panning is not in this range, so it cannot be written with `Y`** (set it with `i`*n*) | 0-255 |
| OPM | `00H`-`FFH`. However, **`14H` cannot be written** (below) | 0-255 |

**Only on SSGS does the register number also select the set.** SSGS is two SSGs forming one device, and the chip itself selects the set by the number. The track's channel does not select a set implicitly. GPIO (`0EH` `0FH` `1EH` `1FH`; `1FH` is the LED on the board) and the unconnected numbers between the volume and panning groups (`23H` `27H` `2BH` `2FH`) cannot be written.

Writing out of range is `Illegal function call`.

#### The mask in the third argument

Writing `Y`*r*`,`*d*`,`*m* sets register *r* to the following value.

```
r ← (current value of r AND m) OR d
```

Bits where *m* is 1 keep the current value, and bits where it is 0 take the value of *d*. When one register packs several parameters, you can specify only the bits you want to rewrite. `Y`*r*`,`*d* without *m* is the same as *m*=0, and the whole register becomes *d*.

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"Y$30,$50,$0F")   ' changes only the OPLLEX voice to 5, keeps the volume
```

**The current value is "the value the chip holds now", including what notes and volume have written.**
None of the Y8960 sound chips can read back their registers, so the BASIC extension keeps a record of its writes.

#### Interaction with notes, volume and voices

Values written with `Y` also go into the BASIC extension's record. So when notes, `V` or `@` write the same register, the following happens.

- **The bits that notes, `V` and `@` are responsible for are rewritten the next time they act.** Even if you change the voice with `Y`, the next `@` sets the voice of that `@`
- **The bits they are not responsible for keep the value written with `Y`.** They do not change even when notes or volume write to the same register
- **Even the bits they are responsible for keep the value written with `Y` until they are rewritten.** Writing only the volume does not revert a voice changed with `Y`

```basic
CALL MTRK(0,0,"@3V15C4Y$30,$50V12C4")   ' the second C uses voice 5, volume V12
```

**What notes, `V`, `@` and `i` are responsible for on OPM.** Notes: the key code and key fraction (`28H`-`37H`) and key-on (`08H`). `V`: the TL of the operators that are audible in the voice. `@`: each register of the voice and bit5-0 of `20H`-`27H`. `i`: bit7-6 of `20H`-`27H`.

#### OPL2EX `04H` cannot be written

`04H` is the mask for four interrupt sources, and two of them, ADPCM playback end and buffer empty, **must always remain masked.** If they are unmasked, the cartridge keeps the interrupt line low with nobody to release it, and the machine stops without any error. Specifying it is `Illegal function call`.

#### OPM `14H` cannot be written

`14H` is the register that enables the timer interrupts; enabling them sends interrupts that nobody handles to the MSX computer. Specifying it is `Illegal function call`.

## Voice data

### FM voice

Same as MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2, except that the low 2 bits of offsets 21 and 29 select the waveform. OPLLEX and OPL2EX tracks read voices in this format.

### OPM voice

32 bytes. OPM tracks read voices made with `VOICE COPY` in this format. The values are the chip's register values as they are, and their direction is also as in the registers.

| Offset | Bits | Content |
|--:|---|---|
| 0 | 7 | Noise (effective only on channel 7) |
| 0 | 5-3 | FB |
| 0 | 2-0 | Connection (CON) |
| 1 | 5-4 | AMS |
| 1 | 2-0 | PMS |
| 2 | 7-0 | Transpose. Signed number of semitones |
| 3 | 7 | Make operator 4 sound |
| 3 | 6 | Make operator 3 sound |
| 3 | 5 | Make operator 2 sound |
| 3 | 4 | Make operator 1 sound |
| 4-10 | | Operator 1 (M1) |
| 11-17 | | Operator 2 (C1) |
| 18-24 | | Operator 3 (M2) |
| 25-31 | | Operator 4 (C2) |

Operator (7 bytes).

| Offset | Bits | Content |
|--:|---|---|
| +0 | 6-0 | TL |
| +1 | 7-6 | KS |
| +1 | 4-0 | AR |
| +2 | 7 | AMS-EN |
| +2 | 4-0 | D1R |
| +3 | 7-6 | DT2 |
| +3 | 4-0 | D2R |
| +4 | 7-4 | D1L |
| +4 | 3-0 | RR |
| +5 | | Unused. Write 0 |
| +6 | 6-4 | DT1 |
| +6 | 3-0 | MUL |

Panning is not part of the voice. `i`*n* determines it.

### SCC waveform

32 bytes × 16 waveforms. Offsets 0-31 are the 32-byte waveform data (Wave level).

### Software envelope

4 bytes. Offset 0 is AR (0-32), 1 is DR (0-32), 2 is SL (0-15), 3 is RR (0-32). For their meaning, see "[Software envelope](#software-envelope--en)".

### ADPCM waveform

Same as MSX-AUDIO (internal representation).
